title: ‘Devastating’: Western Australia fears a black swan moment as bird flu threatens flagship species
text:
When the black swans start dying, Western Australians will know that bird flu has truly arrived.
The birds are an “indicator species” because once they are infected with the H5N1 virus, they are more likely to die than survive, according to the University of Queensland virologist Kirsty Short.
“If avian influenza gets into a place where there are black swans … then I think we will see swan mortality and if there’s a significant number of swans, significant mortality.”
WA’s black swans are deeply woven into its identity. As the state’s official bird emblem, the species is emblazoned on buildings, stamps, the flag and the coat of arms.
Now the bird that has come to define the west is facing devastating consequences.
Unlike many birds, black swans lack a key immune protein involved in recognising viral infections, a difference that may leave them vulnerable to a killer inflammatory response.
The species has been ranked as “very high risk” of becoming infected with the virus, according to a commonwealth national risk assessment.
Experts don’t yet know how black swans will respond to living with a virus that, once established, is expected to circulate and evolve in wild bird populations.
Black swans live in both coastal and inland freshwater areas and can form large colonies when breeding. An infected bird could cause an entire colony to die out, the ornithologist Floyd Holmes from Phoenix Environmental Sciences says.
“It is not likely to wipe out all of the swans, but for any local groups of swans, particularly in the south-west, that all congregate and breed in a single place, the potential to just lose that entire population all at once is definitely there,” Holmes says.
“It would be pretty devastating for that local area.”
South Australia, where the virus was first reported, has already reported three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns. Holmes says the public is also more likely to notice the impacts on black swans because the birds are so large and distinctive.
Nine weeks after a migratory bird brought H5N1 to WA shores – and five years after this variant of the virus reached North America – the WA government says it is now testing the vaccine in five endangered black cockatoos at Perth zoo.
“The feasibility of vaccination in black swans is being explored,” the WA environment minister, Matthew Swinbourn, says. “This is just one tool in the fight against the disease.”
The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, says the government has spent $113m on bird flu preparedness, including purchasing $2m worth of vaccine to protect captive populations of priority species.
The vaccine is produced by US animal health company Zoetis and was originally designed for use in chickens. It is not registered for use in wildlife and would need to be assessed before its use can be extended to native birds, Swinbourn says.
The government was tight-lipped about the strength of evidence that the vaccine will work in native species.
“The vaccination rollout led by states and territories has commenced and will continue across the country in the coming weeks and months,” a Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry spokesperson says.

Birds require two doses of the vaccine, weeks apart, so it is not feasible to vaccinate most wild populations, experts say. Efforts have begun to vaccinate 5,000 little penguins in wild colonies in Victoria, a process only considered possible because the colonies are well-studied, used to humans and return to the same burrows every night.
Short says until now, there has been a lack of investment in research to understand what avian influenza and avian vaccines do in native species.
“There were some studies that were done vaccinating different birds in a zoo with a H5N1 vaccine, and they found that parrots didn’t mount a very good antibody response for some reason,” Short says.
“So there are obviously species-dependent variations, and I think we really should have invested in understanding what this virus means specifically for Australia.”
The BirdLife Australia waterbird ecologist Lindall Kidd says WA is now playing catch up after much of its bird flu preparedness funding was directed towards agriculture.
“Our birds are already under pressure from habitat loss through land clearing and climate change, we could be looking at death by a thousand cuts,” she says.
“There was a known gap in preparedness prior to the bird flu incursion, and we did not have enough plans in place especially for some of our more common, widely spread species. They are the ones in our urban areas, like pelicans and swans,” Kidd says.
She says the psychosocial effect of losing large numbers of swans will be “massive”.
For the Noongar people of south-west WA, the black swan is called Maarli or Kuljak and it carries a totemic significance that predates its adoption as a state symbol, according to Murdoch University Noongar researcher Glen Stasiuk.
“With connections to brotherhood and the seasons, it is a very important bird,” Stasiuk says.
While the future of WA’s bird emblem remains unknown, Holmes puts the possibilities simply.
“Option one is they develop an immunity to the virus, option two is that the virus doesn’t end up reaching all of them, or option three is we lose them all,” Holmes says.
“I suspect that the number of swans is going to go down. Hopefully it doesn’t reach zero. I don’t think it will, but I guess time will tell.”
